title: NLRB v. Hearst Publications, Inc. (1944)
summary: The Board's determination that newsboys are employees under the National Labor Relations Act must be accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law.
notes:
Key line: "[T]he Board's determination that specified persons are 'employees' under this Act is to be accepted if it has 'warrant in the record' and a reasonable basis in law." Justice Rutledge, for the Court.

Citation: 322 U.S. 111 (1944).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was the National Labor Relations Board, which had found that full-time newsboys were employees and ordered the publishers to bargain with their union. Respondents were four Los Angeles newspaper publishers: Hearst Publications, Inc., publisher of the Examiner and the Evening Herald and Express; Stockholders Publishing Co., publisher of the News; and Times-Mirror Co., publisher of the Times. The Los Angeles Newsboys Local Industrial Union No. 75 had sought certification. The publishers refused to bargain on the ground that the newsboys were independent contractors and not their employees.
sections.Material Facts: The newsboys sold the papers on the streets of Los Angeles. The Board found that the full-time newsboys worked continuously and regularly, relied on their earnings to support themselves and their families, and had their total wages influenced in large measure by the publishers, who set the buying and selling prices, fixed their markets and controlled their supply of papers. The publishers' district managers supervised the newsboys' hours and efforts, assigned corners, and furnished sales equipment and advertising materials. The publishers argued that under common-law tests the newsboys were independent contractors because they bought papers and bore the risk of unsold copies. Section 2(3) of the Act said the term employee shall include any employee, without further definition.
sections.Procedural History: The union filed four representation petitions. After a consolidated hearing the Board found the regular full-time newsboys to be employees, designated bargaining units and ordered elections, which the union won. When the publishers refused to bargain, the Board found violations of sections 8(1) and 8(5) and ordered bargaining. The Ninth Circuit, one judge dissenting, set aside the orders, holding that the statute imported common-law standards under which the newsboys were not employees. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed on April 24, 1944.
sections.Issue: The National Labor Relations Act protects the organizing and bargaining rights of employees and defines the term only by saying that employee shall include any employee. The publishers argued that the word carries its common-law meaning, under which the newsboys were independent contractors. The Board applied the statute's purposes to the economic facts. Is the term employee in the Act limited by common-law master and servant standards, and may a court set aside the Board's determination that newsboys are employees when that determination is supported by the record and has a reasonable basis in law?
sections.Holding: The term employee is not confined to common-law standards or to local law but takes its meaning from the history, terms and purposes of the Act and the economic facts of the relationship. The Board's determination that specified persons are employees is to be accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law. The Board's conclusion that the newsboys were employees met that test, and its unit determinations were within its discretion. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Rutledge first rejected the common-law test. The employee and independent contractor distinction varied widely among the states and among purposes, so applying it would make the Act's coverage turn on the accidents of local law rather than on the national problem Congress addressed. The Act is federal legislation administered by a national agency to solve a national problem, so its terms must be read in light of the mischief to be corrected and the end to be attained. Congress meant to reach workers whose inequality of bargaining power and vulnerability to industrial strife created the problems the Act addressed, and those conditions can exist outside the technical master and servant relation. The Court then addressed the division of labor between court and agency. Congress assigned to the Board the task of applying the statute's broad term to the infinite variety of concrete situations. Everyday experience in administering the statute gives the Board familiarity with the circumstances and backgrounds of employment relationships, so its determination, like the determinations of other agencies applying terms such as unfair method of competition, is to be accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law. The Board's findings about the newsboys' dependence, supervision and the publishers' control satisfied that standard, and its decision to define units by tenure rather than function was not an abuse of discretion.

topics.lrs-i-law-fact: Hearst supplies the contested employee-classification example in the law–fact debate.
topics.lrs-i-independent-judgment: The later opinions differ over whether Hearst shows a broad or confined tradition of pre-APA deference.
topics.lrs-i-historical-chevron: Hearst is the pre-Chevron deference precedent that Chevron's framework generalized and Loper Bright reexamined.
topics.lrs-i-delegated-discretion: The Court treated application of 'employee' as a task Congress had primarily assigned to the Board.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 8 to 1. Justice Reed concurred in the result, preferring the coverage test the Board had announced in the Stockholders Publishing decision. Justice Roberts dissented, arguing that Congress used employee in its common and traditional sense, that the question of who is an employee is a question of the meaning of the Act for courts to decide, and that Congress did not delegate to the Board the power to define the employment relationship to promote what the Board saw as the statute's purposes.
